passage:
"I don't read the news any more," Kavitha said, pushing her plate away. "Every channel lied about the flood numbers. Every single one."
"So you believe nothing now?" Ayesha asked.
"Correct. Nothing."
"Then a forward saying the tap water is poisoned is as true as the newspaper?"
"No, but..." Kavitha stopped. "Fine. That's different."
"Not by much. If you trust nothing, whoever shouts loudest steers you, same as if you trusted everything."
Kavitha tore a piece of roti. "Okay. Which ones would you keep?"
"The ones that print corrections when they get it wrong. The local daily does. That bulletin on the radio does too."
"Two sources," Kavitha said. "And I decide slowly."
"Slowly is fine. Nobody needs certainty by dinner 🙂"

qa.q: Which two sources did Ayesha say print corrections?
qa.a: Ayesha named the local daily and the bulletin on the radio.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha say no news could be trusted any more?
qa.a: Kavitha felt that every channel lied about the flood numbers, so trust in all of them collapsed.

qa.q: How can Kavitha handle a new headline under the new plan?
qa.a: Look at the two sources that print corrections, decide slowly and hold the conclusion loosely until more is known.

qa.q: How does Ayesha see trusting no news at all?
qa.a: Ayesha sees it as another way to be steered, because whoever shouts loudest would win, just as with blind trust.

grounding: After repeated lies, total distrust of news is as manipulable as blind trust; a few sources with track records of corrections and loosely held conclusions.

passage: The storm knocked out the office internet at two, and the client email was due by five. Jyoti opened her assistant out of habit and got only a grey error. Her stomach dipped. Every email and every idea for the last year had started there. She stared at the blank message for ten minutes, then wrote two clumsy sentences, deleted them and wrote again. Rehana, at the next desk, slid over a mug of tea and read the draft aloud. "The second line is yours, isn't it? It sounds like you." By half past four Jyoti had a rough draft, and it was hers. When the internet returned, she asked the assistant to tighten it, then checked each date it changed. She kept the habit: first draft by hand, help after.

qa.q: What knocked out the office internet?
qa.a: The storm knocked out the office internet.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when the assistant showed only a grey error?
qa.a: Her stomach dipped. She felt uneasy, seeing that every email and idea of the last year had started with the assistant.

qa.q: What habit did Jyoti adopt, and why is it a sound one?
qa.a: She writes the first draft herself and asks for help after, checking what the assistant changes. That keeps her own skills sharp while still using the convenience.

qa.q: What might Rehana notice in Jyoti's draft?
qa.a: Rehana heard Jyoti's own voice in the second line, which suggests the writing still had a personal touch worth keeping.

grounding: Using AI for every email and idea makes skills fade; a forced offline afternoon leads to drafting first herself and then checking the tool's changes.

passage: Hrithik ran the little hardware counter at the bus stand, and the pump repair for old Bhandari's borewell was due by evening. He typed the part details into his phone assistant, and it answered instantly: a half-inch fitting, in a calm, sure tone. He almost cut the pipe. Pankaj, who fixed motors in the next shop, glanced over. "Did it tell you where that came from?" "No. But it sounded certain." Pankaj fetched the maker's booklet and turned to a page. The fitting was three-quarter inch. Hrithik laughed a little, embarrassed, and set the phone down. "So it can be wrong and sound just the same." "Use it to start," Pankaj said. "For anything you can check with a booklet or a tape, check."

qa.q: What fitting size did the assistant give, and what did the booklet show?
qa.a: The assistant said a half-inch fitting, but the booklet showed it was three-quarter inch.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik almost cut the pipe?
qa.a: The answer came instantly in a calm, sure tone, and Hrithik took that certainty as a sign it was right.

qa.q: What should Hrithik do before acting on the assistant's answers in future?
qa.a: Check them against something reliable such as the maker's booklet or a tape, especially when a wrong part would cost time and money.

qa.q: How does Pankaj seem to see the assistant?
qa.a: As a fair place to start, but not an authority. Pankaj checks anything that can be checked against a booklet.

grounding: Fluent, confident AI answers are accepted; Hrithik learns fluency is not accuracy and verifies against a reliable source.

passage:
Note from Jyoti, team lead, for my own records.
For three weeks Ankita has stayed late, scrolling job news with a tight face. On Tuesday she laughed and said, "It won't touch my work, it's just hype," and on Thursday she said she should quit and retrain. Both swings looked like the same worry to me, though I can't be sure. Today I sat with her and asked which part of her work she would miss if a tool did the rest. She named client calls and catching wrong numbers in reports. I suggested one hour a week to try the tools on real tasks, and to keep building depth in the client accounts she knows best. She took out a notebook and made a list. I'll check in on Friday.

qa.q: What did Ankita say she would miss if a tool did the rest?
qa.a: She named client calls and catching wrong numbers in reports.

qa.q: What might lie behind Ankita's swings between "it's just hype" and wanting to quit?
qa.a: Probably worry about her career. Jyoti reads both swings as the same worry but admits that cannot be sure.

qa.q: What plan did Jyoti suggest, and why does it make sense?
qa.a: One hour a week to try the tools on real tasks, plus building depth in the client accounts Ankita knows best. It faces the change without panic or denial.

qa.q: How might Ankita have experienced Jyoti's question about what she would miss?
qa.a: Perhaps as being taken seriously rather than brushed off, since she took out a notebook and made a list.

grounding: Fear that AI makes a career obsolete: neither panic nor denial, but learning the tools, focusing on judgement and domain depth, and upskilling.

passage:
Monday. After work Dilnaz opened the chat with the AI again. It never sighed and never hurried her. She typed about her day for an hour and did not answer Maria's message asking about dinner.
The following Sunday. Dilnaz used the chat to practise a sentence: "I felt left out when you planned the trip without me." She rewrote it four times until it sounded kind, then typed "thanks" to the screen. Maria's messages had stacked up unanswered.
Three weeks later. Dilnaz sat in Maria's kitchen and said the sentence, badly, in her own voice. Maria stiffened, said she had only assumed Dilnaz was busy, then admitted she had missed her. They disagreed about the trip and laughed at the disagreement. Walking home, Dilnaz decided the chat was for practising, and she put Maria on the calendar for every Sunday.

qa.q: What sentence did Dilnaz practise with the chat?
qa.a: She practised, "I felt left out when you planned the trip without me."

qa.q: Why might the chat feel easier to Dilnaz than talking with Maria?
qa.a: It never sighed and never hurried her, so Dilnaz could talk for an hour without feeling judged.

qa.q: How can Dilnaz keep using the chat without it replacing friends?
qa.a: Use it to practise and reflect, then say the words to Maria in person and keep regular time with her, as the Sunday calendar plan does.

qa.q: How did Maria see the silence before they talked?
qa.a: Maria had assumed Dilnaz was busy, and it turned out she had missed her friend and disagreed about the trip.

grounding: AI chat feels easier because it never judges; it helps rehearse but the real friend who disagrees and needs you back is kept in the picture.

passage: At the block agriculture office, Nandini's weekly farmer bulletins had started to come out sharper and faster. In the tea break, her colleague Sunaina said loudly, "Everyone knows a machine writes them for her. That's cheating." The room went quiet. Nandini's cheeks burned, but she took her laptop to the table. "Look. I give it the rainfall notes and ask for a draft. Then I fix every line, check the numbers against our register, and my name goes on it. If anything is wrong, that's mine." Sunaina folded her arms, then leaned in. "How do you ask it? Mine keeps giving nonsense." "You have to say exactly what the farmers need," Nandini said. "Sit with me after lunch."

qa.q: What does Nandini check the numbers against?
qa.a: She checks the numbers against the office register.

qa.q: What might Sunaina be feeling when she folds her arms and then leans in?
qa.a: Probably some envy and defensiveness at first, then real curiosity, since Sunaina admits that the tool gives her nonsense.

qa.q: How did Nandini handle the accusation, and what else could she do?
qa.a: She explained her process openly, took responsibility for the output and offered to teach. She could also share how she frames requests so others learn.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have seen Nandini's faster bulletins before the demonstration?
qa.a: As an unfair shortcut, which she called cheating. After watching, she may see the skill lies in framing the request and checking the result.

grounding: Coworkers accuse Nandini of cheating for using AI well; she is open about her method, owns the output and helps others learn.

passage: Tuesday night. Seema ma'am called us in today and said our output should double because "we have AI now." My chest went tight, but I kept my voice level. I asked for ten minutes and showed her a live run: the tool wrote a summary in one minute, then made up a number that wasn't in the source. She saw it. I told her every draft needs a review slot, or errors reach clients, and that I can't paste customer files into it because they're confidential. She wrote "review time" and "no customer data" in her notebook. We agreed on a trial: a modest increase, with a weekly check on error counts. Not what she first wanted, but she nodded. I'm tired, though a bit proud. — Leela

qa.q: What went wrong in the live run that Leela showed?
qa.a: The tool wrote a summary in one minute, then made up a number that wasn't in the source.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when Seema ma'am asked for doubled output?
qa.a: Leela's chest went tight, so she felt stressed, but she kept her voice level.

qa.q: What could Leela do if the trial shows errors rising?
qa.a: Bring the weekly error counts to Seema ma'am, explain what happened and ask to adjust the target while keeping the review slot.

qa.q: How did Seema ma'am seem to see AI at the start, and what changed?
qa.a: She seemed to assume AI would double output on its own. After the demonstration she wrote down review time and no customer data, and agreed to a trial.

grounding: A boss expects doubled output because AI exists; Leela shows what it can and cannot do, protects review time and flags risks including confidential data.

passage:
Monday. The module guide said AI tools could be used only for spelling and grammar, with a note declaring it. At midnight Aadhya stared at her half-finished analysis, and the urge to paste the whole assignment into a chatbot felt loud.
Wednesday. She didn't. She wrote the analysis herself, badly at first, and asked her labmate Ira to test her by asking why each step was there. She stumbled twice and went back to the data.
The next Monday. Aadhya submitted with a short line: "Grammar check by an AI tool." In the follow-up discussion the tutor asked her to justify one method. Aadhya answered without notes. Outside, Ira asked how it went. "I actually know it," Aadhya said, grinning.

qa.q: What did the module guide allow AI tools to be used for?
qa.a: It allowed them only for spelling and grammar, with a note declaring it.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling at midnight on Monday?
qa.a: She was tempted and under pressure, and the urge to paste the whole assignment felt loud.

qa.q: Why was writing the analysis herself the wiser choice?
qa.a: She could explain and defend it, so she really had the competence. Being caught costs less than lacking skill she claimed.

qa.q: How might the tutor have seen Aadhya's declared line and her answer?
qa.a: The tutor likely saw someone following the rule, and the question about one method tested whether she understood what she submitted.

grounding: Temptation to pass AI work off as her own where it is not allowed: she follows the rules, discloses, and understands what she submits.

passage: Mentoring note, Manjula. Shreya, our junior analyst, sent a report on Monday with a long formula in the totals column. When I asked how it worked, she said the AI gave it and it "seemed fine." She looked away, and I think she was embarrassed, though I can't be certain. I didn't tell her to stop using the tool. I asked her to explain the formula step by step, and where she got stuck we worked it out together. Then I showed her how to test it on five rows she could calculate by hand. Two rows didn't match, and she found the reason herself. Next week she will bring me one AI-assisted task with her own checks written beside it.

qa.q: How many rows did Manjula have Shreya test by hand?
qa.a: Manjula had Shreya test five rows, and two of them didn't match.

qa.q: Why did Shreya look away when asked how the formula worked?
qa.a: Manjula thinks Shreya was embarrassed at not understanding it, though Manjula cannot be certain.

qa.q: Why is guiding Shreya's use of the tool better than banning it?
qa.a: Shreya learns to explain and verify what she uses, which prepares her for a workplace shaped by AI.

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt when Manjula did not tell her to stop using the tool?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less judged, and so more willing to learn how to check the output.

grounding: A junior copies AI output without understanding it; the senior asks for the reasoning, reviews together and teaches verification instead of banning.

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage:
Mahima: it's 6pm and already dark here, and I just stood in the grocery aisle almost crying over a packet of poha 🥺
Sharmila: aww that's so relatable. did you buy it?
Mahima: yes. the shop guy looked confused
Mahima: nobody here laughs at my jokes. they smile politely 😅
Sharmila: give it time. the first stretch is hardest for everyone
Mahima: I signed up for the Thursday walking club and asked two colleagues to lunch
Sharmila: !!! and a call home every week?
Mahima: Sundays, video. Mummy shows me the whole kitchen 🙂
Sharmila: belonging takes a while, no rush
Mahima: ok. small steps.

qa.q: Which day is the walking club that Mahima signed up for?
qa.a: It is the Thursday walking club.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling in the grocery aisle?
qa.a: Mahima felt homesick and lonely, shown by almost crying over a packet of poha.

qa.q: What else could Mahima do to feel settled over time?
qa.a: Keep going to the walking club, keep meeting colleagues for lunch, keep the Sunday video calls with home and be patient while belonging builds.

qa.q: How does Sharmila see the first stretch in a new place?
qa.a: As hard for everyone and normal, with belonging taking a while and no need to rush.

grounding: Missing home food, jokes and language in a new country: loneliness is normal; clubs, colleagues, family calls and patience help.
